items.stem: What is the difference between val and var in Kotlin?

options.text: val declares a read-only reference; var declares a reassignable one
options.rationale: val cannot be reassigned after initialisation; var can.

options.text: val is for numbers and var is for strings
options.rationale: Both work with any type; the difference is reassignability.

options.text: val values are always compile-time constants
options.rationale: const val is a compile-time constant; plain val need not be.

options.text: var is immutable and val is mutable
options.rationale: It is the reverse: val is read-only.

items.explanation: val cannot be reassigned after initialisation; var can.

items.stem: Select TWO expressions that safely handle a nullable String? named s in Kotlin.

options.rationale: The safe call returns null instead of throwing when s is null.
The Elvis operator supplies a default when the safe call yields null.
Calling a member directly on a nullable type is a compile error.
The not-null assertion throws if s is null, so it is not safe.

items.explanation: The safe call returns null instead of throwing when s is null.

items.stem: Why use a data class rather than a normal class for a simple value holder in Kotlin?

options.text: It auto-generates equals, hashCode, toString and copy from the properties
options.rationale: Data classes synthesise these members based on the primary-constructor properties.

options.text: It makes all properties mutable automatically
options.rationale: Mutability depends on val/var, not on being a data class.

options.text: It prevents the class from being used in collections
options.rationale: Data classes work well in collections.
Null safety is unaffected by data classes.

items.explanation: Data classes synthesise these members based on the primary-constructor properties.
